{{short description|Linear operator on dense subset of its apparent domain}}
{{no footnotes|date=October 2025}}
In [[mathematics]] &ndash; specifically, in [[operator theory]] &ndash; a '''densely defined operator''' or '''partially defined operator''' is a type of partially defined [[function (mathematics)|function]]. In a [[topology|topological]] sense, it is a [[linear operator]] that is defined "almost everywhere".  Densely defined operators often arise in [[functional analysis]] as operations that one would like to apply to a larger class of objects than those for which they ''[[A priori and a posteriori|a priori]]'' "make sense".{{clarify|what’s a priori make sense?|date=August 2024}}

A [[closed operator]] that is used in practice is often densely defined.
==Definition==
Let <math>X,Y</math> be [[Topological vector space|topological vector spaces]].

A '''densely defined''' linear operator <math>T</math> from <math>X</math> to <math>Y</math> is a linear operator of type <math>T: D(T) \to Y</math>, such that <math>D(T)</math> is a [[Dense set|dense subset]] of <math>X</math>. In other words, <math>T</math> is a [[partial function]] whose [[Domain of a function|domain]] is dense in <math>X</math>.

Sometimes this is abbreviated as <math>T : X \to Y</math> when the context makes it clear that <math>T</math> might not be defined for all of <math>X</math>.

== Properties ==
{{Math theorem
| name = Closed Graph Theorem
| math_statement = If <math>X, Y</math> are Hausdorff and metrizable, <math>T : D(T) \to Y</math> is densely defined, with continuous inverse <math>S : Y \to D(T)</math>, then <math>T</math> is closed. That is, the set <math>\{(x, T(x)): x \in D(T)\}</math> is closed in the [[product topology]] of <math>X \times Y</math>.
}}

{{Math proof
|proof=Take any [[Net (mathematics)|net]] <math>(x_\alpha)</math> in <math>D(T)</math> with <math>T x_\alpha\to y</math> in <math>Y</math>. By continuity of <math>S</math>, <math>x_\alpha = S(Tx_\alpha)\to\ S(y)</math>. Hence there exists some <math>x \in D(T)</math> such that <math>x_\alpha\to x</math>, and <math>T x = T(S(y)) = y</math>.
}}

The [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff property]] ensures sequential convergence is unique. The [[Metrizable space|metrizability property]] ensures that [[Sequential space|sequentially closed]] sets are closed. In functional analysis, these conditions typically hold, as most spaces under consideration are [[Fréchet space]], or stronger than Fréchet. In particular, [[Banach space|Banach spaces]] are Fréchet.

==Examples==

=== Sequence ===
Let <math>X=\ell^{2}(\mathbb N)</math> be the [[Hilbert space]] of [[Square-summable sequence|square-summable sequences]], with orthonormal basis <math>(e_n)_{n\ge 1}</math>. Define the [[diagonal operator]]
:<math> A : D(A)\to \ell^{2}, \qquad x_n \mapsto nx_n,</math>
with domain
:<math>D(A):=\Big\{x=(x_n)_{n\ge 1}\in \ell^{2}:\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{2} | x_n|^{2}<\infty\Big\}.</math>
Then <math>D(A)</math> is dense in <math>\ell^2</math> because the [[Finite support|finitely supported sequences]] <math>c_{00}\subset D(A)</math>, and <math>c_{00}</math> is dense in <math>\ell^2</math>. The operator <math>A</math> is closed and [[Unbounded operator|unbounded]], since <math>\|Ae_n\|_2=n</math>.

There exists a bounded inverse:
:<math>A^{-1}:\ell^{2}\to D(A),\qquad (A^{-1}y)_n:=\frac{y_n}{n},\qquad \|A^{-1}\|=\sup_{n\ge 1}\frac{1}{n}=1.</math>
Hence <math>A:D(A)\to \ell^{2}</math> is bijective with bounded inverse, so <math>0\in\rho(A)</math> and, by the [[Neumann series]] argument, the [[resolvent set]] of <math>A</math> contains the open unit disk <math>\{\,\lambda\in\mathbb C:\ |\lambda|<1\,\}</math>.

In fact, the spectrum of <math>A</math> (that is, the complement of its resolvent set) is precisely the set of positive integers, since for any <math>\lambda \not\in \{1, 2, \dots\}</math>, the diagonal formula
:<math>(A-\lambda I)^{-1}y=\bigl(\tfrac{y_n}{n-\lambda}\bigr)_{n\ge 1}
</math>
defines a bounded operator <math>\ell^2\to D(A)</math>.

Thus, <math>A</math> is a densely defined, closed, unbounded operator with bounded inverse and nontrivial, unbounded spectrum.

=== Differentiation ===
Consider the space <math>C^0([0, 1]; \R)</math> of all [[Real number|real-valued]], [[continuous function]]s defined on the unit interval; let <math>C^1([0, 1]; \R)</math> denote the subspace consisting of all [[Smooth function|continuously differentiable functions]].  Equip <math>C^0([0, 1]; \R)</math> with the [[supremum norm]] <math>\|\,\cdot\,\|_\infty</math>; this makes <math>C^0([0, 1]; \R)</math> into a real [[Banach space]].  The [[Differential operator|differentiation operator]] <math>D</math> given by <math display="block">(\mathrm{D} u)(x) = u'(x)</math> is a linear operator defined on the dense linear subspace <math>C^1([0, 1]; \R) \subset C^0([0, 1]; \R)</math>, therefore it is a operator densely defined on <math>C^0([0, 1]; \R)</math>.

The operator <math>\mathrm{D}</math> is an example of an [[unbounded linear operator]], since 
<math display="block">u_n (x) = e^{- n x} \quad \text{ has } \quad \frac{\left\|\mathrm{D} u_n\right\|_{\infty}}{\left\|u_n\right\|_\infty} = n.</math>
This unboundedness causes problems if one wishes to somehow continuously extend the differentiation operator <math>D</math> to the whole of <math>C^0([0, 1]; \R).</math>

=== Paley–Wiener ===
The [[Paley–Wiener integral]] is a standard example of a [[continuous extension]] of a densely defined operator.

In any [[abstract Wiener space]] <math>i : H \to E</math> with [[Adjoint of an operator|adjoint]] <math>j := i^* : E^* \to H,</math> there is a natural [[continuous linear operator]] (in fact it is the inclusion, and is an [[isometry]]) from <math>j\left(E^*\right)</math> to <math>L^2(E, \gamma; \R),</math> under which <math>j(f) \in j\left(E^*\right) \subseteq H</math> goes to the [[equivalence class]] <math>[f]</math> of <math>f</math> in <math>L^2(E, \gamma; \R).</math>  It can be shown that <math>j\left(E^*\right)</math> is dense in <math>H.</math>  Since the above inclusion is continuous, there is a unique continuous linear extension <math>I : H \to L^2(E, \gamma; \R)</math> of the inclusion <math>j\left(E^*\right) \to L^2(E, \gamma; \R)</math> to the whole of <math>H.</math>  This extension is the Paley–Wiener map.
